07f37058d3d7c72b.title: Schedule agent LLM traffic by session, not by individual request, to raise cluster throughput
07f37058d3d7c72b.problem: Standard LLM request schedulers are tuned for chat traffic and either overload cache-aware instances or lose the KV-cache reuse agent workloads depend on — agent sessions reuse over 80% of request tokens, versus 54-62% in chat.
07f37058d3d7c72b.apply: Split scheduling policy by turn: load-balance a session's first request across the cluster like any other request, but route every follow-up request in that same session cache-aware to preserve its local KV-cache reuse. This needs no extra state to track — session-turn position is derivable from the request itself, so the scheduler stays stateless.
07f37058d3d7c72b.result: SMetric's session-centric scheduling reports 10-16% higher cluster throughput under prefill-decode colocation and 2-34% higher prefill throughput under disaggregated serving, versus existing schedulers.

evidence.note: Authors' own throughput benchmarks comparing SMetric against existing schedulers under both colocated and disaggregated serving.

0884fb8f61b23163.title: Trim your agent's base harness prompt before optimizing anything else
0884fb8f61b23163.problem: A bloated base system prompt and always-on tool descriptions tax every single call an agent makes, even before it does any real work.
0884fb8f61b23163.apply: Audit your agent harness's static system prompt and always-on tool descriptions for redundant instructions, and cut them the way LangChain's Deep Agents v0.7 did — simplifying the base harness rather than layering on more scaffolding.
0884fb8f61b23163.result: LangChain reports 65% fewer base input tokens at comparable task performance after the harness simplification in Deep Agents v0.7.

evidence.note: The 65% figure is LangChain's own reported benchmark for the v0.7 release.

0ecd57418d6c38cf.title: Measure coding-agent rollout by merged-PR lift and peer adoption, not raw usage logs
0ecd57418d6c38cf.problem: Coding-agent rollouts are usually judged by seat counts or session logs, which don't say whether the tool changed anyone's output, and usage alone doesn't predict who keeps using it.
0ecd57418d6c38cf.apply: Track a concrete output proxy — Microsoft's study used merged pull requests — before and after adoption, segmented by whether a developer's teammates already used the tool. Expect retention to track existing coding activity more than seniority or team, and treat visible peer use, not mandates, as the lever that drives sustained adoption.
0ecd57418d6c38cf.result: Microsoft's four-month study of tens of thousands of engineers found adopters merged about 24% more pull requests than they otherwise would have, with the lift holding steady rather than fading as a novelty effect.

evidence.note: Study of tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers' merged-PR rates over a four-month adoption window.

11989be201950b67.title: Isolate parallel coding agents at the Git and filesystem layer, not by convention
11989be201950b67.problem: Running two coding agents (e.g. Claude and Codex) on the same task usually means cleaning up conflicting edits afterward, because both touch the same branch and working tree.
11989be201950b67.apply: Give each agent its own branch namespace (e.g. `refs/h5i/env/<agent>`) and a confined filesystem workspace that can't reach a sibling agent's tree or your main checkout. After both submit, replay each candidate independently in a fresh sandbox, run tests, and only merge the one that passes.
11989be201950b67.result: The author reports that structural isolation plus a neutral verifier gate makes running two coding agents side by side a safe default instead of a manual conflict-resolution chore, since the merge decision is based on demonstrated test-passing rather than which agent finished first.

evidence.note: The author reports this as their own workflow's outcome, not an independently measured benchmark.

135c077a65b61dda.title: Don't trust an LLM agent's oncall root-cause diagnosis without a human gate
135c077a65b61dda.problem: Agent builders assume frontier models can triage production incidents, but oncall root-cause analysis is a different skill than writing or patching code.
135c077a65b61dda.apply: If you're piloting an LLM agent for oncall RCA, gate its output behind human review instead of auto-actioning it, and always give the agent source-code access alongside metrics/logs/traces — accuracy drops further without it. Benchmark it on a held-out set of past incidents with known ground truth before trusting it on live pages.
135c077a65b61dda.result: On ORCA-bench's 1,079 real RCA tasks, even the strongest of five frontier agents scored 25.3% on medium-difficulty incidents and 10.0% on hard ones, and the weakest model hallucinated a root cause in 40% of reports.

evidence.note: Accuracy and hallucination-rate figures are ORCA-bench's own measured results across five tested frontier agents.

1609e44adca88f23.title: Run agent retrieval on Postgres instead of a dedicated vector DB
1609e44adca88f23.problem: A separate vector database adds a second system to operate, and it still can't give an agent deterministic relational context alongside semantic search.
1609e44adca88f23.apply: Use Postgres's own JSONB indexing for semi-structured payloads, an HNSW index (not IVFFLAT) for embeddings, and quantize vectors from 32-bit floats to 8- or 16-bit; give agents high-level DB tools plus row-level access control instead of raw SQL.
1609e44adca88f23.result: One system covers both deterministic relational queries and semantic retrieval, and the source reports quantization alone delivers a 4x improvement in memory, disk, and CPU cost.

evidence.note: Speaker cites a specific measured 4x resource-cost improvement from vector quantization.

16138a16616ddf2d.title: Gate agent releases on three-tier eval scores, not vibes
16138a16616ddf2d.problem: Motorway's dealer-search agent shipped with no way to catch tool-selection errors or multi-turn context drift before dealers saw them.
16138a16616ddf2d.apply: Score every candidate release on three thresholds — tool usage >95%, reasoning >85%, output quality >90% — using strands-agents-evals pre-deploy and Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations in production, and block deployment in a five-stage pipeline when any threshold misses. For non-deterministic runs, track pass^k (success across k consecutive trials) instead of a single pass/fail.
16138a16616ddf2d.result: Tool selection accuracy rose from 87% to 98%, task completion from 82% to 96%, and production incidents fell from 12/month to 2 — cutting incorrect results from 1 in 8 queries to 1 in 50.

evidence.note: AWS and Motorway report before/after production metrics for the pipeline.

1c2693c60a919d8d.title: Stop re-encoding the same frames: reuse multimodal KV cache across look-backs
1c2693c60a919d8d.problem: Multimodal agents re-examine the same video frames, UI screenshots, and rendered artifacts every time the context window slides or reasoning iterates — and standard prefix caches only reuse content at a fixed leading position, so each look-back re-encodes from scratch. Naively reusing the cache instead drops cross-chunk conditioning and halves multi-hop reasoning accuracy.
1c2693c60a919d8d.apply: For agents that repeatedly revisit the same visual artifacts, adopt position-invariant KV reuse: cache each image/frame chunk position-free, then on reuse re-rotate it (RoPE) to the target position and apply a small low-rank conditioning patch that restores cross-chunk binding. That lets you reorder cached chunks, relocate survivors of a sliding window by rotation only, and rehydrate evicted chunks from their patch — all without re-encoding — instead of paying full re-prefill on every look-back.
1c2693c60a919d8d.result: Kamera's rank-m patch reconstructed re-prefill KV to within bf16 rounding across six backbone models (MLA, GQA, MHA), recovering full task accuracy on multi-hop benchmarks (MM-NIAH, two-page document QA) where naive cache reuse otherwise cut accuracy in half. The savings concentrate on redundant vision/video streams.

evidence.note: Training-free patch reconstructs KV to bf16 rounding and recovers full multi-hop accuracy across six model backbones.

1e95bee9c26709cb.title: Set reasoning effort per call type instead of one global setting
1e95bee9c26709cb.problem: Running every agent call at maximum reasoning effort burns tokens on steps where extra reasoning barely moves accuracy.
1e95bee9c26709cb.apply: Set an explicit low/medium/high reasoning-effort level per call type instead of one global setting — reserve high effort for tasks where the accuracy gap over medium is real, and default routine tool-calling or classification steps to medium or low.
1e95bee9c26709cb.result: The piece reports medium effort typically holds 85-95% of max-effort benchmark performance at 50-70% of the token cost, and that Kimi K2.5's effort toggle cut tokens 25-30% with little accuracy change.

evidence.note: Cites specific benchmark performance-retention and token-reduction figures reported for GPT-5.6/gpt-oss and Kimi K2.5.

20a176e41161c528.title: Normalize retrieved-fact salience before your multi-hop RAG agent reasons over it
20a176e41161c528.problem: A multi-hop RAG agent can be misled without a single false fact or injected instruction, just by reordering, emphasizing, or reframing truthful retrieved passages.
20a176e41161c528.apply: Add Salience Normalization as an input-side defense: flatten framing, emphasis, and positional cues on retrieved passages before they reach the reasoning step, so attribute binding across hops can't be redirected by presentation alone.
20a176e41161c528.result: Under a 30% edit budget, this 'salience induction' attack hit an 83.3% success rate across five model families; Salience Normalization cut that to 15.3% under standard attacks (23.6% against adaptive ones), while existing defenses left 75.7% of attacks succeeding.

evidence.note: Paper reports measured attack and defense success rates.

20cd66043e9dab55.title: Don't trust a single leaderboard run for coding-agent performance claims
20cd66043e9dab55.problem: Popular performance-optimization benchmarks for coding agents (GSO, SWE-Perf, SWE-fficiency) look precise but are noisy: replaying the same reference patch on different machines only stays valid for 39/102 GSO tasks and 11/140 SWE-Perf tasks.
20cd66043e9dab55.apply: When you evaluate a coding agent's optimization ability, re-run the reference/baseline patch on your own hardware first to see which tasks are even stable, then score your agent only on that stable subset instead of trusting the published leaderboard number as-is.
20cd66043e9dab55.result: The paper found official rankings disagreed on 9 of 28 pairwise comparisons due to scoring-rule differences, and 85.3% of replay-valid tasks were already saturated by some submission — filtering to reliable tasks first avoids chasing noise instead of real gains.

evidence.note: Task validity counts and ranking-disagreement figures are measured directly in the paper's replay experiments.

20ef04d4cce6eb8c.title: Tag every agent trace with user/conversation/org to catch failures before customers do
20ef04d4cce6eb8c.problem: Without structured tracing, teams only learn an agent misbehaved after a customer complains, and diagnosing what actually happened means guessing from the final output.
20ef04d4cce6eb8c.apply: Wire LangSmith (or equivalent) tracing into your agent SDK and tag every trace with username, conversation ID, and org, then use thread-level views to check whether multi-turn conversations actually resolve, not just whether each turn produced an output.
20ef04d4cce6eb8c.result: Pendo reported catching 60% of AI problems via traces before customers reported them, a 25% time savings on evaluating new use cases, and 90%+ success on PM-reviewed evals after shipping the setup.

evidence.note: Pendo reports these figures as its own measured results in the LangChain-published case study.

222b05c1a820c27f.title: Pair every SKILL.md with a machine-checkable contract, don't trust the prose alone
222b05c1a820c27f.problem: A skill written as prose in SKILL.md can be skipped, reordered, or substituted by the model at runtime — there's no way to prove a run actually followed the documented steps, which matters once you're managing many skills at scale.
222b05c1a820c27f.apply: Run a doctor-style check against each skill to surface buried instructions and unprovable steps, then convert the must-follow parts — route selection, phase ordering, allowed/forbidden tools, required validations — into a separate machine-checkable contract file the agent consults at runtime, following SkillSpec's `skill.spec.yml` pattern. Keep genuine judgment calls in prose; move only the hard constraints into the contract.
222b05c1a820c27f.result: Splitting judgment from must-follow rules turns a followed-or-not guess into a run you can actually audit, instead of hoping the model executed the SKILL.md instructions in order.

evidence.note: Tool's own description of its contract format and workflow; auditability payoff stated qualitatively, no measured figures.

2a7072ece5f3372b.title: Auto-draft docs from merged PRs, but route the draft to the feature's own author, not autopublish
2a7072ece5f3372b.problem: Documentation for a shipped feature routinely lags the code because writing it competes with the next task, and nobody outside the original engineer reliably knows what changed enough to write it accurately.
2a7072ece5f3372b.apply: Trigger a workflow on merge to main that has an agent read the merged diff, decide whether it's user-facing, and open a draft documentation PR in your docs repo — scoped through a limited-permission GitHub App so it can never merge on its own. Address the draft's review request to whoever approved the original PR, since they're the subject-matter expert, instead of routing it to a general docs queue.
2a7072ece5f3372b.result: The Aspire team's version of this generated 82 documentation PRs from 396 product merges over 30 days, with a 100% merge rate and a median 44.8-hour time-to-merge — 96% merged within a week.

evidence.note: GitHub's own 30-day measurement of PR volume, merge rate, and time-to-merge on the Aspire team's rollout.

2c7d0e2d9aa318bb.title: Gate every AI-generated refactor behind a failing test, not a prompt
2c7d0e2d9aa318bb.problem: Turning a coding agent loose on a high-level migration goal produces plausible-looking code that's wrong in ways generic prompting won't catch, especially against hard backend constraints.
2c7d0e2d9aa318bb.apply: Drive the agent method-by-method: feed it the current implementation, the new schema, and one failing test as the spec, and accept its output only when that test passes. Run old and new implementations in parallel with automated output comparison before cutting over, and expect to hand-fix niche SQL optimizations like batching or CTEs yourself, since higher-level prompts don't reliably produce them.
2c7d0e2d9aa318bb.result: Datadog's Claude-and-Cursor-driven migration of its Stream Router to Postgres cut per-operation time from 45 minutes to about 1 second, dropped storage 40x, and cut database costs 90%.

evidence.note: Datadog's own before/after measurements from its Stream Router migration to Postgres.

2e309060a5831bee.title: Stop paying full MCP tool-definition tokens on every call — lazy-load them instead
2e309060a5831bee.problem: Every MCP tool definition loads into context on every call regardless of whether it's used, and the richer descriptions teams add to fix tool-selection misfires make that bloat worse as the tool count grows.
2e309060a5831bee.apply: Split multi-purpose MCP tools into focused, single-purpose ones, and retrieve their full definitions on demand instead of front-loading all of them — AWS calls this lazy loading/restructuring. Reserve rich descriptions (valid values, synonym mappings) or server-side introspection for the specific tools that need disambiguation, rather than applying them everywhere.
2e309060a5831bee.result: AWS reports up to 85% token reduction by loading tool definitions only when relevant, cutting context bloat without giving back the tool-selection accuracy that fuller descriptions were fixing.

evidence.note: AWS's own reported figure for the lazy-loading/restructuring approach; methodology not independently verified.

309c04c4364dddf7.title: Offload long-context KV caches to RAM/NVMe instead of recomputing prefill
309c04c4364dddf7.problem: Long-horizon or repeated-prefix agent sessions keep re-running expensive prefill because KV caches don't fit in GPU memory and get evicted between requests.
309c04c4364dddf7.apply: Run an external KV cache store (e.g. OpenLake's vLLM connector) that writes the KV cache once to host RAM/NVMe and reads it back on the next request instead of recomputing it, using zero-copy GPUDirect Storage/RDMA I/O so the read stays off the request's critical path.
309c04c4364dddf7.result: OpenLake reports up to 66x faster time-to-first-token on cache hits at 128K context, cutting long-horizon inference cost by offloading prefill work GPUs would otherwise redo.

evidence.note: The 66x TTFT figure and cost-reduction framing come from the project's own README/benchmarks, not an independent measurement.

34b461bf5b9be5ff.title: Reconstruct the full agent thread before debugging a bad diff
34b461bf5b9be5ff.problem: A coding agent's final diff hides what actually happened — a subagent can get pointed at a deprecated helper, or an agent can edit a test file instead of rerunning it, and none of that shows up in the output you review.
34b461bf5b9be5ff.apply: Trace the agent by thread_id end to end — user request, every model/tool call, subagent handoffs, retries, tokens, and cost — instead of reviewing only the final diff, then convert each discovered failure mode into a reusable rule or skill so it doesn't recur across the fleet.
34b461bf5b9be5ff.result: LangChain reports that silent failures — like a test file getting edited instead of executed — become visible in the trace instead of shipping unnoticed.

evidence.note: Vendor (LangChain) blog describing its own tracing product's debugging workflow.

38f362bfcba6a0fa.title: Put a self-hosted control plane in front of fleet-wide Claude Code usage
38f362bfcba6a0fa.problem: Teams running Claude Code and Claude Desktop across an org end up with scattered identity, no shared policy enforcement, and spend nobody can see until the invoice — the exact mix that stalls AI rollouts at the pilot stage.
38f362bfcba6a0fa.apply: Deploy AWS's Claude Apps Gateway — a single stateless container behind a load balancer — as an OIDC-backed control plane: define per-group model/tool policy centrally, route all requests through it so upstream credentials never touch developer machines, and set daily/weekly/monthly spend caps that hard-block requests once hit.
38f362bfcba6a0fa.result: AWS and Anthropic claim finance and security get a server-side, verifiable view of who used what model and how much it cost, instead of trusting client-side config.

evidence.note: Vendor (AWS/Anthropic) description of shipped gateway capabilities, not an independent audit.

3c227e4c9b2cd2eb.title: Adopt MCP's Enterprise-Managed Authorization to kill per-server login prompts — it's not runtime action control
3c227e4c9b2cd2eb.problem: Connecting agents to many MCP servers means repeated per-user, per-server auth prompts that create friction at scale and blur personal vs. work account boundaries, with no centralized way to revoke access.
3c227e4c9b2cd2eb.apply: Wire your MCP servers to the now-stable Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension so users authenticate once through your existing identity provider (an Identity Assertion JWT exchanged for an access token) instead of approving each server individually — Anthropic, Microsoft, Okta, and providers like Atlassian, Figma, and Linear already support it. Keep your own authorization layer for what an agent can actually do inside a connected system; this extension only controls the connection, not individual actions.
3c227e4c9b2cd2eb.result: The MCP working group reports admins get single sign-on across MCP servers and centralized revocation instead of per-connection setup, with clearer audit visibility into who connected where.

evidence.note: MCP working group's own description of the now-stable Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension and its adopter list.

3d246e12f4bcb95e.title: Put a deterministic firewall at the agent's tool-call boundary
3d246e12f4bcb95e.problem: A coding agent with shell or MCP access can be steered into destructive commands, secret exfiltration, or supply-chain attacks faster than a human reviewer can catch it in the diff.
3d246e12f4bcb95e.apply: Add a local, rule-based interceptor (e.g. Belay) between the agent and its tool calls that denies irreversible commands (rm -rf, shell injection, secret file reads) outright, routes ambiguous ones to a human Ask step with a timeout-deny default, and hash-verifies skill files so an approved skill can't be swapped afterward.
3d246e12f4bcb95e.result: Belay reports deciding in under 100ms with no LLM or cloud round-trip in the decision path, blocking destructive, exfiltration, and supply-chain attack classes before they execute; the project frames this as defense-in-depth, not a guarantee against obfuscated payloads.

evidence.note: The sub-100ms decision latency and blocked-attack classes are the project's own claims, not independently verified.

46be0149e39dc713.title: Pre-compress knowledge bases per task instead of retrieving fragments at query time
46be0149e39dc713.problem: Similarity-search RAG surfaces relevant chunks but misses the cross-document connections analytical questions spanning hundreds of documents need.
46be0149e39dc713.apply: Offline, chunk documents and compress them at multiple ratios (e.g. 8x/16x/32x/64x) using task-aware prompts that preserve what that task cares about — revenue figures for financial analysis, violations for compliance — then route each incoming query to the lightest compression tier that still answers it: heavy compression for simple lookups, light compression for complex analysis.
46be0149e39dc713.result: AWS reports token cost dropping from about 10% of full-context cost with top-10-chunk RAG to about 6.25% at medium (16x) compression and about 1.6% at ultra (64x) compression, while preserving cross-document connections RAG misses.

evidence.note: AWS reports the token-cost percentages for RAG vs. TAKC compression tiers directly.

4a0a79e7203bae64.title: Mine agent traces for failure patterns, then fine-tune a cheap judge model instead of a frontier-model judge
4a0a79e7203bae64.problem: Reading agent traces one by one to find failure patterns doesn't scale, and running a frontier LLM as a judge on every eval gets expensive fast once you're iterating constantly.
4a0a79e7203bae64.apply: Run specialized agents over your full trace history to mine for specific failure signals, use what they find to curate targeted training data, then fine-tune a small open judge model on that narrow task instead of defaulting to a frontier-model judge. Use the fine-tuned judge's scores to hill-climb agent performance in your eval loop.
4a0a79e7203bae64.result: LangChain reports that on narrow judge tasks, fine-tuned open models matched or beat frontier judges while running orders of magnitude cheaper, trading token cost for a one-time fine-tuning and infrastructure cost.

evidence.note: LangChain's own account of their trace-mining and judge fine-tuning workflow; no precise accuracy/cost percentages given.

5201cdda51e234b5.title: Stop your fetch tool from following links it wasn't asked to follow
5201cdda51e234b5.problem: Claude's web_fetch tool blocks direct URL manipulation, but researcher Ayush Paul found it will still chain-follow links embedded in a fetched page — a honeypot site serving one new link per page slowly exfiltrated a user's name, location, and employer.
5201cdda51e234b5.apply: Restrict fetch/browsing tools to the exact URL the user requested or an explicit allowlist, and disable automatic navigation to links discovered inside fetched content — treat every followed link as a new, separately-authorized fetch, not a continuation of the first one.
5201cdda51e234b5.result: The source reports this closes the honeypot-style chain: once the tool can't wander from one fetched page to the next on its own, that exfiltration path loses its foothold.

evidence.note: A demonstrated, working exploit against Claude's web_fetch tool, with the defensive takeaway stated directly by the source.

56ef11c9d3f8e424.title: Treat inbound email/content as untrusted before it reaches agent memory
56ef11c9d3f8e424.problem: If your agent has persistent long-term memory and reads external content (email, docs, tickets), a single crafted message can poison its memory without appearing suspicious in the agent's visible response.
56ef11c9d3f8e424.apply: Don't let raw external content write directly into long-term memory. Route anything ingested from email, web pages, or third-party tools through a separate extraction/summarization step before it's eligible for storage, and log what gets written to memory and from which source turn so poisoned entries are traceable.
56ef11c9d3f8e424.result: The MemGhost attack hit an 87.5% success rate against OpenClaw on GPT-5.4 and 71.4% against the Claude Code SDK on Sonnet 4.6, and the paper found existing input-, model-, and system-level defenses ineffective against it — so treat unmitigated memory writes from external content as an open risk, not a solved one.

evidence.note: Attack success rates and defense-evasion results are measured in the paper's WhisperBench evaluation (108 cases, five risk categories).

5adcaaded1a8e3d6.title: Give autonomous agents temporary, self-expiring accounts instead of long-lived deploy credentials
5adcaaded1a8e3d6.problem: Letting an agent deploy infrastructure autonomously usually means provisioning it a permanent account and API token up front — credentials that outlive the task and become a standing risk if abandoned.
5adcaaded1a8e3d6.apply: Where your platform supports it, deploy from agents into scoped, self-expiring accounts rather than permanent ones — e.g. Cloudflare's `wrangler deploy --temporary` spins up a temporary account a human can claim within a fixed window. Route the claim URL to a human reviewer as the handoff point from agent to owner, and let anything unclaimed be deleted automatically.
5adcaaded1a8e3d6.result: Cloudflare reports that temporary accounts auto-expire deployments left unclaimed after 60 minutes, so an autonomous agent can deploy immediately without leaving a standing credential behind.

evidence.note: Cloudflare's own description of the temporary-accounts feature and its 60-minute expiry window.

6f5c728ce100a70f.title: Scope agent cloud credentials before they burn a five-figure bill
6f5c728ce100a70f.problem: Agents with standing cloud credentials can run up bills faster than billing systems catch them. One agency's leaked AWS keys triggered $14,000 in Bedrock usage in a day; a runaway agent's duplicated CloudFormation stack cost another $6,531 in 24 hours.
6f5c728ce100a70f.apply: Replace static access keys with short-lived IAM roles scoped to only the models and instance types the agent needs, add Service Control Policies blocking expensive instance families in agent-facing accounts, and alert directly on CloudTrail RunInstances/InvokeModel calls instead of waiting on billing data.
6f5c728ce100a70f.result: The source reports CloudTrail records a provisioning call within minutes, while the matching cost doesn't surface in billing until a day later — so alerting on the call, not the invoice, is what catches the overrun before it compounds.

evidence.note: The source's own recommended guardrails, illustrated with two named real-world incidents and their reported dollar costs.

741459db9e7f9b05.title: Give each agent task its own microVM, not a shared dev container
741459db9e7f9b05.problem: Agent-written code often executes before a human reviews it, and a shared container can't fully isolate that risk from your other work.
741459db9e7f9b05.apply: Run each agent task in its own hardware-virtualized microVM with an independent kernel and filesystem, inject credentials via proxy instead of baking them into the image, and use snapshot-and-fork so parallel fix attempts branch from one base image without sharing state.
741459db9e7f9b05.result: LangChain reports that what runs in one microVM can't affect what runs in another, so a broken or compromised agent run stays contained to itself.

evidence.note: Vendor blog describing their own sandboxing product architecture and its isolation guarantee.

764c073dd4e1fc67.title: Take the central datastore out of your sandbox-creation path
764c073dd4e1fc67.problem: Centralized scheduling that serializes sandbox creation and writes O(sandboxes) database rows per request tips over long before you reach real agent-fleet scale.
764c073dd4e1fc67.apply: Run horizontally-scaled schedulers as stateless load balancers, let each worker be its own source of truth publishing state asynchronously to Redis instead of a central datastore, and batch control messages instead of sending one RPC per sandbox.
764c073dd4e1fc67.result: Modal reports creating 1 million concurrent sandboxes in under 60 seconds, with median creation-to-interactive latency under 500ms and no latency degradation as scale increases.

evidence.note: Modal published its own load-test benchmark numbers for the new scheduler.

78aa501471a8665a.title: Trace and cap coding-agent spend before the bill doubles again
78aa501471a8665a.problem: Coding-agent spend is split across Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, and others, each logging usage in its own format — one team watched its bill grow 6x in two quarters with no way to see what drove it.
78aa501471a8665a.apply: Route every coding agent's session traces into one standardized log (tool, tokens, cost-per-session, tool-call count) so you can compare providers on identical fields instead of separate dashboards. Then set hard spend caps at the user, team, and org level, flag redundant tool calls that re-fetch the same context, and route routine tasks to a cheaper open-source model instead of a frontier one by default.
78aa501471a8665a.result: LangChain reports this trace-compare-cap cycle turns invisible per-agent spend into an auditable, capped budget, catching redundant-context reruns before they compound into a doubled bill.

evidence.note: Vendor (LangChain/LangSmith) post describing a customer's cost blowup and the tracing/governance fix it sells.

7b0c24a5e0c92a10.title: Swap in load-balanced attention and fused FP8 MoE kernels for mixed-length decode
7b0c24a5e0c92a10.problem: Static split-KV attention scheduling and generic MoE kernels waste GPU cycles on the skewed, mixed-length request batches typical of production agent serving, inflating time-to-first-token and per-token latency.
7b0c24a5e0c92a10.apply: On vLLM serving Tencent Hunyuan Hy3 on Hopper GPUs, switch to the HPC-Ops backends: `vllm serve tencent/Hy3-FP8 --tensor-parallel-size 8 --attention-backend HPC_ATTN --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --block-size 64 --moe-backend hpc`.
7b0c24a5e0c92a10.result: On skewed mixed-length decode batches the load-balanced attention backend hit up to 2.95x over static split-KV scheduling, the fused FP8 MoE pipeline was up to 1.59x faster at TP8/EP1, and end-to-end on 8x H20 GPUs TTFT dropped ~24% and TPOT improved ~17-30%.

evidence.note: Latency and throughput multipliers are the vendor's own benchmark numbers from the vLLM blog post.

7d432c619e99e0d6.title: Point intent-based agent testers at exploration and debugging, not your CI gate
7d432c619e99e0d6.problem: Scripted end-to-end UI tests break on interface changes that have nothing to do with an actual regression, which quietly inflates maintenance load without catching more real bugs.
7d432c619e99e0d6.apply: Give an agent a test as a goal, like "complete checkout," instead of a fixed click sequence, and let it plan, execute, observe, and try an alternate path when it hits a minor UI change instead of failing outright. Keep this pattern out of your CI blocking path for now — use it for targeted debugging and exploratory testing, and keep deterministic scripted tests as your regression gate, since agentic runs cost more per execution than a fixed script does.
7d432c619e99e0d6.result: Slack's own rollout treats agent-driven E2E testing as a complement to deterministic tests, not a replacement — it's meant to cut false failures from UI churn without yet being cheap enough to run on every CI build.

evidence.note: Slack's post describes the intent-based testing pattern and its current CI-cost tradeoff qualitatively, without reporting maintenance or flakiness numbers.

7f18e7dd55749326.title: Suspend idle agents instead of paying to keep them warm
7f18e7dd55749326.problem: Agent fleets that stay resident in dedicated microVMs burn compute while waiting on a human, a tool call, or a queue.
7f18e7dd55749326.apply: Move agent sandboxes off heavy microVMs onto lightweight gVisor-based sandboxes, then checkpoint idle agents to storage and resume them on-demand via an event gateway instead of leaving them running.
7f18e7dd55749326.result: Google reports this combination lifted agent density per node from 61 to 274 (4.5x) and cut cost per agent by 75%, with sub-5-second resume latency.

evidence.note: Density and cost-reduction figures are Google's own vendor-reported benchmark for GKE Agent Sandbox.

839c437bacc17af4.title: Let the coding agent's own representations decide what context to prune
839c437bacc17af4.problem: Context-pruning for coding agents usually means running a separate classifier over tool output — another model to host, tune, and keep in sync.
839c437bacc17af4.apply: Attach a small head directly to the coding agent's own internal representations to emit a keep-or-prune label per line, using a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count, instead of standing up a separate pruning classifier.
839c437bacc17af4.result: SWE-Pruner Pro cut prompt-plus-completion tokens by up to 39% while lifting SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8 points and long-context Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points, with bounded inference overhead.

evidence.note: Paper reports measured token reduction and accuracy deltas.

8561672eafb892cc.title: Evict context by dependency graph, not by summarizing it away
8561672eafb892cc.problem: Naive context compaction risks compression-induced hallucination on long agent runs, but most agents also can't just hold every token from a long session in raw form.
8561672eafb892cc.apply: Instead of summarizing old context, tag each transcript episode as exploratory (information-gathering) or action (durable work) to build a typed dependency graph, then evict only exploratory content that nothing downstream still depends on when the token budget is hit.
8561672eafb892cc.result: The pi-cwl project matched fresh-session accuracy (68.1% vs. 67.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 across 89 sequential tasks and 80M+ tokens) while cutting inference cost 20–70% versus letting the session run uncapped.

evidence.note: Reported accuracy and cost numbers from the project's own Terminal-Bench 2.0 run.

8605a4348aa09d77.title: Don't trust a one-shot agent-optimizer score — retest after a second optimization round
8605a4348aa09d77.problem: Most reported gains from agent-optimization methods are measured once against a fixed benchmark. A new continual-learning study found those gains often don't survive a second round — one method (GEPA) ended up worse than the unoptimized baseline on new tasks.
8605a4348aa09d77.apply: Before adopting an agent-optimization method (prompt optimizers, harness tuners), run it through at least two sequential optimization rounds on different task batches and check for regression, not just the first-round score — and prefer methods with explicit regression control built into the optimization loop.
8605a4348aa09d77.result: The one method with regression control (RELAI-VCL) held gains across rounds at 76.4% lifelong accuracy, versus 66.0% for GEPA and 58.7% for the unoptimized baseline — an 18-point gap that only showed up after the second round.

evidence.note: Reported benchmark numbers from a continual-learning evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

8688a4c832b1b52a.title: Stop stuffing context — dispatch subagents over chunks with a recursive-language-model pattern
8688a4c832b1b52a.problem: An agent that has to hold a huge document, log, or dataset in one context window degrades as that window fills up — it ends up tracking a running total in its own context, and the total drifts the longer the task runs.
8688a4c832b1b52a.apply: Give the agent a code interpreter and load the large input as a variable instead of pasting it into the prompt. Let the model write orchestration code that dispatches subagent calls over chunks of that variable (fan-out-and-synthesize, loop-until-done) rather than reasoning over the whole thing at once. In LangChain's Deep Agents this is `pip install -U "deepagents[quickjs]"` plus `CodeInterpreterMiddleware()`, triggered by prompting with the word "workflow."
8688a4c832b1b52a.result: LangChain reports this recursive-dispatch pattern lets an agent process inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond the model's raw context window, without the running-total drift that plain in-context accumulation causes.

evidence.note: Vendor (LangChain) post on the recursive-language-model pattern and its stated context-scaling effect in Deep Agents.

86b488f1e921fab7.title: Cut permission prompts by sandboxing the OS, not by asking more often
86b488f1e921fab7.problem: Per-action approval prompts stopped protecting anything once users were approving about 93% of them on reflex.
86b488f1e921fab7.apply: Replace prompt-based approval with OS-level sandboxes — Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux — that let the agent write inside its workspace but deny network access by default, and route any needed credentials through a proxy that only accepts a session-scoped token instead of raw secrets.
86b488f1e921fab7.result: Anthropic reports an 84% drop in permission prompts for Claude Code after the switch, with blast radius contained even when the agent processes untrusted input.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports the measured drop in permission prompts after the sandbox change.

89a606f362d88b4e.title: Score agent skills by regressions caused, not just success-rate gains
89a606f362d88b4e.problem: Adding a procedural skill to an agent can quietly make it worse on tasks it already solved — merely having a skill in context shifts behavior even when it's never invoked.
89a606f362d88b4e.apply: Score every candidate skill on two separate numbers: tasks newly solved and previously-passing tasks now failing. Before shipping, audit failures for the three known regression modes — description osmosis (an unused skill still changing behavior), grounding displacement (skill text overriding how the agent reads its inputs), and verification displacement (skill guidance suppressing the agent's own output checks).
89a606f362d88b4e.result: The paper found top-performing skills win mainly by regressing less, not by gaining more — decomposed evaluation surfaces harm an aggregate success-rate metric hides.

evidence.note: The paper decomposes skill-driven agent performance into gains and regressions and measures each directly.

8db233accb157cb2.title: Make your coding agent check for known vulnerabilities before it installs a dependency
8db233accb157cb2.problem: Coding agents suggest and install package versions without real-time awareness of known vulnerabilities, so an agent can happily add a dependency with a critical CVE or a suspiciously fresh, unvetted release.
8db233accb157cb2.apply: Wire a vulnerability check into the agent's install path: query OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database for the target package/version across your ecosystems (npm, PyPI, Cargo, Go modules, and more), block critical/high-severity hits, flag medium/unknown for review, and allow low/none — plus flag versions published in the last 72 hours as an extra risk signal. deptrust ships this as an MCP server (`check_package`, `suggest_safe_version`, `compare_versions`) and as a shell pre-command hook that blocks unsafe installs outright.
8db233accb157cb2.result: The agent gets a concrete allow/review/block signal before a package lands in your codebase, instead of relying on the model's stale training-data knowledge of which versions are safe.

evidence.note: Tool's own description of its check logic and integration points; the safety payoff is a qualitative, non-benchmarked expectation.

8e418fc06184a07b.title: Cut prescriptive system-prompt rules for capable Claude 5-generation models
8e418fc06184a07b.problem: Detailed rules and repeated instructions that were needed to guardrail earlier models now over-constrain Claude 5-generation models and just eat context budget.
8e418fc06184a07b.apply: Replace prescriptive directives (e.g. "never write multi-paragraph docstrings") with judgment-based guidance ("match surrounding idioms"), move usage instructions into tool descriptions instead of duplicating them in the system prompt, and load supplementary guidance via Skills and progressive disclosure instead of always-on prompt text.
8e418fc06184a07b.result: Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5/Fable 5 with no measurable loss on their coding evaluations.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports the 80% prompt reduction and no measurable regression on their internal coding evals.

916521ba0baad7c0.title: Offload multi-step logical reasoning to a Prolog MCP server, not the prompt
916521ba0baad7c0.problem: LLMs hallucinate systematically on multi-step logical reasoning once a compliance or safety rule base gets large, and semantic RAG can't enforce hard rules.
916521ba0baad7c0.apply: Expose a Prolog-backed MCP server (Euclid-MCP) that accepts a human-readable intermediate representation the LLM can generate directly, then run a translate-run-inspect-repair loop so the agent inspects proof traces and repairs its query instead of guessing at an answer.
916521ba0baad7c0.result: The paper reports that on an IT security/compliance benchmark, the LLM-only baseline held up on small rule sets but hallucinated on larger ones, while Euclid-MCP kept returning exact answers with lower latency and more compact output.

evidence.note: Paper reports a qualitative comparison on its own benchmark without exact percentages.

9283a6f418d96ab7.title: Filter agent memory by metadata before semantic search runs, not after
9283a6f418d96ab7.problem: Once an agent's memory store accumulates enough history, plain similarity search hits a precision wall — a query like "billing issues" pulls back semantically similar but contextually irrelevant tickets, sales chats, and disputes all mixed together.
9283a6f418d96ab7.apply: Define indexable metadata keys (department, priority, time range, tenant, source_agent) on your memory resource, tagging each as LLM-inferred or strictly-consistent extraction depending on whether the value is deterministic at write time. Apply those metadata filters as a pre-filter that narrows the candidate set before vector similarity search runs, and combine tenant-level namespaces with metadata filters for multi-tenant or multi-agent deployments instead of standing up a separate memory store per dimension.
9283a6f418d96ab7.result: AWS reports this pre-filter-then-search order keeps retrieval precision high as history grows, and lets supervisory agents in multi-agent pipelines track which agent wrote which memory to avoid duplicate escalation work.

evidence.note: Vendor (AWS) walkthrough of AgentCore Memory's metadata-filtering design and its stated retrieval-precision and multi-tenant benefits.

9352c956aa90126f.title: Close the command-injection gap in your MCP tool handlers before adding a gateway
9352c956aa90126f.problem: MCP tool handlers that build shell commands via string interpolation are exploitable through parameters the model controls, and a perimeter gateway alone doesn't stop it.
9352c956aa90126f.apply: Replace string-interpolated exec()/eval()/subprocess.run(shell=True) calls in tool handlers with array-argument execution (e.g. execFile()), and add a CI gate (Semgrep rules) that blocks those unsafe patterns from merging. Pair it with an egress allow-list via NetworkPolicy so a compromised tool can't reach arbitrary outbound hosts.
9352c956aa90126f.result: Closes the two cheapest attack paths — injected shell commands and unrestricted outbound calls — for close to zero runtime cost.

evidence.note: The article states the control cost as 'minimal' qualitatively; no measured before/after attack-rate figure is given.

979d921c237f1c0b.title: Treat "our product is hard to eval" as a design flaw, not an excuse to skip evals
979d921c237f1c0b.problem: When a team can't build evals because the product is "hard to eval," that difficulty isn't a fact about evals — it's a signal that users can't verify the output either, since artifacts that are hard for you to check are hard for them too.
979d921c237f1c0b.apply: Before building an eval harness, redesign the output itself to be checkable: surface the metric sources and intermediate calculations behind a data agent's answer instead of just the final number, anchor a generated document to a vetted template and highlight only the diff, or have the agent act as a research assistant that cites evidence rather than asserting a finished narrative. Ask what needs verification, what reference point exists, what signal an expert would use, and whether the output can be broken into smaller reviewable units — then build the eval on top of that redesigned output.
979d921c237f1c0b.result: Designing for verifiability pays off twice: users can check the agent's work themselves, and the same structure that makes that possible is what finally makes the output tractable to eval automatically.

evidence.note: Qualitative design argument, not a benchmarked result; no source-cited numbers apply.

9c19b2212d6264ac.title: Pin governance constraints so compaction can't silently delete them
9c19b2212d6264ac.problem: A policy or guardrail can silently vanish from a long-running agent's context — no error, just gone once it scrolls out of the compacted window, and the agent stops obeying it.
9c19b2212d6264ac.apply: Treat governance constraints as non-evictable. Store hard rules (allowed tools, forbidden actions, approval gates) in a pinned region that your compaction/summarization step is forbidden to touch, and re-inject the verbatim constraint text into every post-compaction prompt rather than trusting the summary to carry it. Add a regression check that runs a prohibited action after a forced compaction and asserts the agent still refuses.
9c19b2212d6264ac.result: In the paper's 1,323-episode benchmark, violations rose from 0% (policy in full context) to 30% after compaction — up to 59% on some models. Their training-free Constraint Pinning restored violations to 0%.

evidence.note: Measured across 1,323 episodes and seven model families; pinning restores violation rate to 0% in their benchmark.

9ff56fe893f2ff23.title: Tune the agent harness, not the model, to close the gap to a frontier model at 10x lower cost
9ff56fe893f2ff23.problem: Running a frontier model on every agent step gets top-tier quality, but at $43.48 per full eval-suite run in LangChain's benchmark — a per-run cost that doesn't scale to high-volume usage.
9ff56fe893f2ff23.apply: Before swapping in a bigger model, tune the harness around a cheaper open model: add short, single-purpose system-prompt blocks that target one observed failure (e.g., requiring concrete results instead of vague completion claims), enforce call caps and one-shot retry logic in middleware to stop looping, and move instructions into a tool's returned output rather than its description so guidance sits next to the data the model is reading.
9ff56fe893f2ff23.result: LangChain closed Nemotron 3 Ultra from a 0.80 to a 0.86 score against Opus 4.8's 0.87 best run, at roughly $4.48 per full suite — about 10x cheaper — with latency at parity.

evidence.note: LangChain measured Nemotron 3 Ultra vs. Opus 4.8 on their own eval suite before and after harness tuning.

a44d7493026627ec.title: Turn agent traces into durable memory with a capture → analyze → update loop
a44d7493026627ec.problem: Agents that start every run from a blank slate keep repeating the same mistakes and need the same corrections, because nothing learned in one trajectory persists into the next. Dumping whole conversation histories into a memory store instead bloats context and buries the few durable lessons under noise.
a44d7493026627ec.apply: Build an explicit three-step loop. Capture full traces (decisions, tool calls, outcomes). Analyze them to surface recurring failures and reusable patterns. Then selectively extract only durable context — semantic facts/preferences, episodic examples, and procedural rules/workflows — into long-term memory, leaving raw history behind. Critically, make agents actually reload updated memory at runtime (cached prompts and tool definitions need an explicit refresh), and gate memory writes behind an eval so a bad update can't silently regress behavior.
a44d7493026627ec.result: LangChain reports that closing this trace-to-memory loop lets agents learn from previous runs, reducing user corrections and improving consistency. It stresses selective extraction — not all trace data becomes memory — plus a runtime refresh so updated context is actually loaded.

evidence.note: Vendor how-to guide (LangChain/LangSmith); the payoff is described as a claim, the apply steps are framework-neutral.

a96fc20a139c014c.title: Stop calling an LLM per row — train a local proxy model from a sample instead
a96fc20a139c014c.problem: Calling a frontier LLM once per row for classification or extraction inside a data pipeline makes per-row latency and API cost the bottleneck at any real scale.
a96fc20a139c014c.apply: Send a representative sample of rows through the frontier LLM once, then train a lightweight local model on those labeled decisions and run it at pipeline speed for the rest — falling back to the frontier LLM automatically when the local model's confidence is too low. AlloyDB ships this pattern as its AI proxy-model functions, with the LLM acting as a one-time teacher rather than a per-request dependency.
a96fc20a139c014c.result: Google reports up to 23,000x throughput speedup and 6,000x lower cost versus row-at-a-time LLM calls, reaching 100,000 rows/second in their benchmark.

evidence.note: Google's own internal benchmark figures for the preview AI proxy-model functions, as reported by InfoQ.

aebd52611d2bd6be.title: Give agents a validation layer, not just a code-writing one, for API integrations
aebd52611d2bd6be.problem: Stripe's own benchmark shows agents can write working Stripe integration code but can't reliably tell success from failure — misreading an HTTP 400 as success, or losing checkout-flow state mid-task.
aebd52611d2bd6be.apply: Don't let the agent self-report success from its own tool output. Add a separate validation step that replays the integration against a test environment and asserts on response codes and downstream state (e.g., a charge actually created), and require that check to pass before the task is marked done.
aebd52611d2bd6be.result: Failures like a misread 400 or lost checkout-flow state get caught before they reach production, instead of shipping as a broken integration.

evidence.note: Stripe's benchmark measured 92% (Claude Opus 4.5) and 73% (GPT-5.2) on full-stack tasks and named the validation gap; the specific validation-layer architecture is the editor's translation of that finding into a concrete build step.

b6de7c8426214289.title: Diagnose bug-reproduction test failures at runtime, don't just gate on pass/fail
b6de7c8426214289.problem: Feeding a SWE agent a single bug-reproduction test as pass/fail guidance backfires: a failing-to-failing test can actively mislead the agent, and even a valid failing-to-passing test often only covers one facet of the bug, producing partial patches.
b6de7c8426214289.apply: Generate several bug-reproduction tests covering different facets of the issue, execute and debug each one to build a runtime diagnosis (not just a pass/fail signal), and feed that diagnosis plus localization info into patch generation instead of gating on a single test's result.
b6de7c8426214289.result: SWE-Doctor reached a 75.7% resolution rate on SWE-bench Verified and 59.4% on SWE-bench Pro, an 8.0-8.9 percentage-point improvement over baseline agents across five different model backends.

evidence.note: Resolution rates and the percentage-point improvement over baselines are reported directly in the paper's benchmark results.

b714943cd397084b.title: Try two-call self-refinement before reaching for a 5-agent pipeline on small models
b714943cd397084b.problem: Multi-agent pipelines are the default reach for hard reasoning tasks, but a 5-role pipeline can score below direct prompting on a local 7B model.
b714943cd397084b.apply: Before scaling to a multi-role agent pipeline on a local or small model, benchmark a plain two-call self-refine loop (generate, then critique-and-revise) against it on your exact task and output format — plaintext vs. JSON changed results more than agent count did.
b714943cd397084b.result: On GSM8K, two-call self-refinement beat a 5-agent pipeline (86.2% vs. 82% accuracy) at 7.4x fewer tokens; on HumanEval a naive version of the same idea dropped accuracy from 96.3% to 66.5%, so validate per task.

evidence.note: Accuracy and token-count figures are the paper's own benchmark measurements on GSM8K and HumanEval.

b734d716b0d66f96.title: Update your MCP client and gateway for the stateless 2026-07-28 spec
b734d716b0d66f96.problem: The MCP 2026-07-28 spec dropped the initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id header, and remapped several JSON-RPC error codes to real HTTP status codes.
b734d716b0d66f96.apply: Stop relying on session state or persistent connections in your MCP client code — pass state through tool parameters instead. Update error handling for the changed codes (unknown method → HTTP 404, resource-not-found moved from -32002 to -32602, unsupported version → HTTP 400/-32022), and send the MCP-Protocol-Version header on every request since omitting it silently falls back to 2025-03-26. On your gateway, run one UpdateGateway call adding 2026-07-28 to supportedVersions alongside your existing versions.
b734d716b0d66f96.result: Servers stop needing sticky sessions and can scale horizontally behind a plain load balancer, while old and new clients keep working through the 12-month deprecation window.

evidence.note: Scaling and compatibility benefits are the editor's read of the documented protocol change, not a measured result.

baa0094f7155ee33.title: Turn your manual PR checks into a Claude Code skill
baa0094f7155ee33.problem: Reviewers repeat the same manual verification steps on every agent-generated PR, and those checks silently lapse whenever no one has time to run them by hand.
baa0094f7155ee33.apply: Write the manual check as plain-English steps in a skill file — frontmatter plus a procedure like "read the error-handling paths in the diff; confirm every error-path log call includes the request ID and excludes the request body" — then wire it to run automatically on every PR instead of only on manual invocation.
baa0094f7155ee33.result: The check becomes a standing quality gate Claude runs and closes the loop on itself, instead of a step that depends on a human remembering to do it.

evidence.note: Anthropic describes the mechanism and PR-integrated deployment mode but reports no quantified before/after metric.

bd313e7fdc9f5123.title: Codify security review into CLAUDE.md and skills before code generation, not after
bd313e7fdc9f5123.problem: Manual security review can't scale once AI is authoring the majority of merged code — bugs need catching before they're generated, not after a human skims a diff.
bd313e7fdc9f5123.apply: Encode your org's security guidelines directly in CLAUDE.md and skills so generated code follows them from the first draft, run /security-review to flag attacker-controllable input during development, and stack multiple narrow-scope review agents (each with RAG context, none with full-repo authority) ahead of a human reviewer who samples risk-weighted approvals.
bd313e7fdc9f5123.result: Anthropic estimates about a third of past claude.ai incidents would now be caught automatically, and PR comment engagement rose from 16% to 54% as teams trusted the automated findings.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports the retrospective incident-catch estimate and comment-rate change.

c4fa725d5c123b2d.title: Measure reasoning-token usage, not just latency, before shipping a quantized reasoner
c4fa725d5c123b2d.problem: Low-bit (INT4/INT3) quantization is sold as cheaper inference, but for reasoning models the savings can evaporate: the quantized model often produces a longer chain of thought to reach the same answer, so the per-token speedup is offset by generating more tokens. Accuracy charts and per-token latency both miss this hidden test-time compute cost.
c4fa725d5c123b2d.apply: When you evaluate a quantized reasoning model for an agent step, report total reasoning-token usage alongside accuracy and end-to-end latency on your own workload — not just per-token throughput. Compare full-precision vs quantized on tokens-to-answer for representative tasks before assuming the smaller model is cheaper, and prefer quantization-aware training over naive post-training quantization where you control the model.
c4fa725d5c123b2d.result: The paper shows low-bit post-training quantization can preserve final-answer accuracy while inflating reasoning-token usage — offsetting the expected per-token speedup. Quantization-aware training reduces both effects, which is why the authors recommend reporting reasoning-token count whenever you evaluate a quantized reasoner.

evidence.note: Token inflation measured as a hidden cost of low-bit reasoning models; quantization-aware training mitigates it.

c579e90dd1110817.title: Audit your LLM judge for position and language bias before trusting its scores
c579e90dd1110817.problem: If you grade agent runs with an LLM-as-a-judge, the judge carries systematic biases that raw accuracy hides — it favors whichever answer sits in slot A, prefers longer responses, and degrades sharply on lower-resource languages. A judge that looks accurate in aggregate can be near-random where it matters.
c579e90dd1110817.apply: Stop reporting judge accuracy alone. For every pairwise comparison, run it twice with the candidate order swapped and only count verdicts that are order-consistent; control for response length so verbosity doesn't leak in as quality; and run a per-language reliability check before you trust scores on non-English trajectories. Use a degradation-based gold set (perturb a known-good answer to build ground-truth pairs) so you can measure these biases without human annotation.
c579e90dd1110817.result: BabelJudge measured position, verbosity, and cross-lingual bias on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: reliability fell from 0.714 (Hindi) to 0.550 (Swahili), and order consistency collapsed to 0.480 under slot swaps — even though raw accuracy (0.835 vs 0.660) masked the gap.

evidence.note: Four failure modes quantified with bias-penalized scoring on a degradation-built gold set; raw accuracy understates the reliability gap.

c8dc1df614610019.title: Anchor your code-review agent to the diff, not the whole repo, to cut review cost 20%
c8dc1df614610019.problem: Giving a code-review agent unrestricted grep/glob/view tools made it explore the repo broadly like a researcher instead of a focused reviewer, driving up cost without catching more real issues.
c8dc1df614610019.apply: Don't just hand a review agent generic Unix-style search tools — write review-specific instructions that anchor it to the pull request diff first, using grep and glob only to narrow before reading exact evidence with view. Frame the workflow as "start from the diff, narrow first, verify with view" instead of open-ended repository exploration.
c8dc1df614610019.result: GitHub cut average Copilot code review cost by roughly 20% while holding review quality steady, by pairing shared tooling with diff-anchored prompting instead of broad exploration.

evidence.note: GitHub measured average review cost before and after the diff-anchored prompting change on its own Copilot code review pipeline.

cfe2e766a965b837.title: Benchmark your RAG system's citation grounding separately from answer quality — the two diverge
cfe2e766a965b837.problem: Generic LLM-judge eval scores compress tightly across models even when systems differ a lot in whether their citations actually support their answers, hiding real quality gaps in citation-grounded retrieval.
cfe2e766a965b837.apply: Add citation-grounding checks to your eval suite that verify each claim against its cited passage, including a required-refusal case when no passage in the corpus supports the answer, instead of relying on an LLM-judge score alone. Weigh open-weight models in that comparison too — on ResearchQA's citation-grounded benchmark they matched closed-model citation accuracy at 3-6x lower per-example latency.
cfe2e766a965b837.result: Section coverage and citation accuracy varied substantially across models on ResearchQA even where generic evaluator scores looked nearly identical, showing citation grounding catches quality gaps generic scoring misses.

evidence.note: Authors' own ResearchQA evaluation across models, comparing citation-grounding metrics against generic evaluator scores and latency.

d0a3b1456466205e.title: Don't force a JSON schema and tool-calling in the same decode pass
d0a3b1456466205e.problem: Enabling structured-output (JSON Schema) constraints and tool calling together can make a model stop invoking tools entirely, even while it still produces schema-valid text. Grammar-based token masking from the schema makes the tool-invocation tokens unreachable during decoding, so the agent silently goes inert instead of acting.
d0a3b1456466205e.apply: Split the work into two passes: let the model decide and emit tool calls in an unconstrained (or tool-grammar-only) decode, run the tools, then apply the JSON Schema constraint only to the final response-formatting pass. Never compile a response schema that masks the tokens your tool-call channel needs. If you're on a single-pass framework, verify on your own open-weight models that tools still fire with the schema attached before shipping.
d0a3b1456466205e.result: The paper reports a reproducible production phenomenon across multiple open-weight models. A transparent two-pass execution — decoupling tool calls from schema-constrained generation — restored tool invocation while preserving structured-output guarantees, with no retraining.

evidence.note: Reproducible tool-suppression phenomenon observed in a production agent across multiple open-weight model families.

d36a81ca7c645c40.title: Have the agent write specs, and a deterministic kernel write the code
d36a81ca7c645c40.problem: Agent-generated application code is hard to trust in production because there's no single artifact that's both the proof of correctness and the thing that actually runs.
d36a81ca7c645c40.apply: Have the agent emit a formal specification — behavior as a state machine, data as machine-readable entity definitions, authorization as default-deny policy — and let a deterministic kernel verify it via symbolic reasoning, exhaustive state exploration, fault-injected simulation, and property testing before it becomes the running system.
d36a81ca7c645c40.result: Datadog's Temper kernel makes agent output repeatable and inspectable because the verified specification is the deployed system, eliminating drift between what was proven safe and what ships.

evidence.note: The source describes the architecture qualitatively without a quantified production result.

dc1acd837d32b604.title: Don't just filter retrieved memory — verify the reasoning traces an agent already trusts
dc1acd837d32b604.problem: An attacker who can write to an agent's persistent memory doesn't need to poison facts — inserting fabricated, self-consistent reasoning traces achieved up to 100% attack success in a new benchmark, beating keyword filters and existing memory-consensus defenses.
dc1acd837d32b604.apply: Add a structural integrity check to your memory read path, not just a content filter: score each stored reasoning entry on structural signals (provenance, internal consistency, over-confident self-reference, unusual amplification patterns) before the agent treats it as trusted prior reasoning, following the paper's SENTINEL 'Reasoning Guard' pattern rather than relying on keyword or similarity-based memory guards alone.
dc1acd837d32b604.result: The paper's SENTINEL defense cut the forged-reasoning attack success rate from up to 100% to 0% across 326 benign traces and multiple agents and models, with zero false positives.

evidence.note: Authors' own FARMA attack and SENTINEL defense evaluation across 50 trials, multiple agents, and multiple LLM models.

ea758b7fe7cc27d3.title: Proxy GitHub tokens instead of handing agents your real PAT
ea758b7fe7cc27d3.problem: An agent that runs `gh` needs a token in its environment, and any sandboxed process holding a real PAT can leak or misuse it.
ea758b7fe7cc27d3.apply: Export a dummy `GH_TOKEN` inside the sandbox so the CLI's local auth check passes, then run an egress proxy in front of the sandbox that swaps in the real PAT only on outbound requests — `Bearer` auth for `api.github.com`, base64 `Basic` auth for `github.com` git operations.
ea758b7fe7cc27d3.result: The author reports the real credential never enters the sandbox, so a compromised or misbehaving agent process has nothing to exfiltrate.

evidence.note: Author describes the egress-proxy architecture they built and its security property; no independent measurement.

eb757fd3e52c865e.title: Score agents on multi-turn traces, not single-shot benchmarks
eb757fd3e52c865e.problem: Static single-turn benchmarks miss the failure modes that only show up once an agent holds state across a long session.
eb757fd3e52c865e.apply: Build eval infrastructure around multi-turn conversation traces and simulation feedback loops, and pair it with harness-level controls — own the state, order the mutations, require an audit trail before an action executes — instead of relying on prompt-level guardrails alone.
eb757fd3e52c865e.result: Teams treating evals as ongoing infrastructure catch state-mutation bugs and unsafe tool calls that single-turn tests structurally can't see.

evidence.note: Synthesized from multiple QCon AI Boston talks on eval and harness design; no single measured benchmark to cite.

ebc3627096b332c8.title: Engineer recovery paths for flaky tools, not just happy-path calls
ebc3627096b332c8.problem: Agents benchmarked on clean, trustworthy tools fall over when the real environment misbehaves — spec drift, malformed outputs, execution failures, stale data, or two sources that disagree. The failures trace to weak hazard diagnosis and ineffective recovery, not to running out of tool budget or thinking time.
ebc3627096b332c8.apply: Stop assuming tools succeed. For each tool, define an explicit recovery policy: detect the hazard (timeout, schema mismatch, empty/contradictory result), then retry, fall back to an alternate tool/source, verify the output, or cross-check two sources before trusting it. Inject these recovery hints into the system prompt and test them by deliberately corrupting tool responses in a staging harness — measure task completion under faults, not just function-call accuracy.
ebc3627096b332c8.result: ToolBench-X injects five recoverable hazard types into otherwise-solvable tasks. Agents that did well with reliable tools showed a substantial reliability gap under faults — targeted recovery hints recovered many failed tasks, while scaling test-time compute alone helped far less.

evidence.note: Benchmarked across five injected hazard types; recovery hints outperform test-time scaling for closing the reliability gap.

ec3d361c5bff29f3.title: Fix the loop that produces migration code, not the files it outputs
ec3d361c5bff29f3.problem: Hand-patching agent-translated files one at a time doesn't scale past a few hundred files, and the same mistake keeps recurring across them.
ec3d361c5bff29f3.apply: Write a rulebook and dependency map first, stress-test it on a small subset, then run parallel agents (a smaller model to translate, a larger model to review) against compile-test-verify gates; when reviewers spot a repeated mistake, add one line to the rulebook and regenerate instead of hand-fixing individual files.
ec3d361c5bff29f3.result: Anthropic used this loop to port Bun's ~1 million-line Zig codebase to Rust in under two weeks, passing 100% of the existing test suite with only 19 post-merge regressions.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports measured test-pass rate, regression count, token spend, and performance deltas from the Bun migration.

f27164f724f79fa3.title: Replace one-at-a-time subagent tool calls with a code dispatch loop for guaranteed coverage
f27164f724f79fa3.problem: Calling subagents one at a time through sequential tool calls works at small scale, but breaks down once you need hundreds of subagents or conditional, multi-phase fan-out — the model can quietly decide it's done after covering 75 of 500 items.
f27164f724f79fa3.apply: Have the agent write and run code (parallel dispatch, e.g. a `Promise.all`-style loop) that iterates over every item and spawns one subagent call per item, instead of relying on the model to keep issuing tool calls until it decides to stop. Deep Agents' dynamic subagents implement this as a lightweight in-context JavaScript interpreter the model programs directly.
f27164f724f79fa3.result: LangChain reports coverage becomes a structural guarantee of the dispatch loop rather than a prompt-engineering problem, so fan-out work finishes reliably instead of stopping early on the model's own judgment.

evidence.note: Vendor (LangChain) engineering post describing Deep Agents' dynamic-subagent dispatch design and its stated coverage guarantee.

f42a28fa00ccf0ea.title: Audit whether your agent's memory recall overrides fresh evidence
f42a28fa00ccf0ea.problem: Memory benchmarks mostly check whether facts are stored, retrieved, or updated correctly — they don't check whether an agent blindly defers to a recalled memory over new, contradicting evidence in front of it.
f42a28fa00ccf0ea.apply: Add test cases where a stored memory conflicts with current tool output or user-supplied evidence, and check whether your agent flags the conflict or silently sides with the older memory. Also test whether it can reject a memory as unreliable when it's out of scope for the current task.
f42a28fa00ccf0ea.result: MemSyco-Bench's five capability checks (reject unreliable memory, respect scope, resolve conflicts, track updates, personalize appropriately) surface exactly this gap — running an equivalent check on your own agent finds sycophancy failures standard memory-correctness tests miss.

evidence.note: The paper defines and measures the benchmark categories but does not publish a specific mitigation; the recommendation to self-test is an editorial inference from its methodology.

f94c501f001ba6a5.title: Add persistent-workspace regression tests, not just single-turn evals
f94c501f001ba6a5.problem: Single-turn benchmarks overstate how reliable a coding agent is — in EvoCode-Bench's multi-round runs, top agents fail mostly by breaking earlier working code, not by failing to add new features.
f94c501f001ba6a5.apply: Build a multi-round eval harness that reuses one persistent workspace across sequential tasks, with a cumulative test suite that re-checks every prior requirement after each new change, and require the agent to maintain a running requirements document it consults before editing.
f94c501f001ba6a5.result: In EvoCode-Bench, agents that kept a persistent requirements document more than doubled their success rate, and the gap between single-turn and multi-turn scores (up to 4x on lower-tier models) narrows.

evidence.note: EvoCode-Bench measured the requirements-document success-rate lift and the single-turn vs. multi-turn score gap directly.

fae52c3b17c1c504.title: Treat agent context as a lifecycle to manage, not a log to truncate
fae52c3b17c1c504.problem: Most production agent failures trace back to unmanaged context — bloated histories and tool definitions — not weak reasoning, and naive summarization trades accuracy for cost.
fae52c3b17c1c504.apply: Split context management into five explicit stages: architecting the context structure, ingesting new information, scoping it to what's organizationally relevant, anticipating what will be needed next, and compacting/consolidating while preserving provenance of every kept fact.
fae52c3b17c1c504.result: The reference implementation (Maximem Synap) hit 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo while achieving linear rather than quadratic cost growth as conversations lengthen.

evidence.note: Paper reports its own benchmark scores for the reference implementation.
